Commentary.Commentary: We are back for the chase! The New Zealand team are spreading out in the middle as their skipper Mitchell Santner is leading them. There comes the openers of Pakistan, Babar Azam and Saud Shakeel, who is opening in place of Fakhar Zaman, who was out of the field due to an injury and is not allowed to open. Matt Henry will start the proceedings for New Zealand. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Now, Pakistan faces the daunting task of chasing 321 under the lights on what remains a good batting surface. With dew likely to play a role, their batters will need to step up against a well-rounded New Zealand bowling attack. Will Pakistan pull off a successful chase, or will New Zealand's bowlers rise to the occasion and secure their first win of the tournament? The stage is set for an electrifying second innings!

Will Young, one of the centurions for New Zealand is up for a quick chat. He says that it means a lot as it was an important moment for him, scoring the century, especially after they lost early wickets but he did well to form partnerships and held up one end. Mentions about the partnerships between him and Tom Latham as it laid the good platform for a good finish which was helped by a good partnership of Glenn Phillips and Tom Latham. Further adds that hitting on the back of a length balls is hard and it is gripping for spinners on this surface. Concludes it by saying that he thinks that it is a pretty good score to defend on this surface.

On the bowling front, Pakistan struggled to contain the flow of runs. Their key pacer Shaheen Afridi went wicketless, unable to make an impact with the new ball. Haris Rauf with his 2 wickets was the pick of the bowlers, while Naseem Shah and Abrar Ahmed chipped in with a wicket each. However, with little support from the rest of the attack, New Zealand dominated proceedings with the bat. Pakistan have another issue in hand that Fakhar Zaman wont be able to open the batting due to the on field injury he went through.

Young provided a solid foundation at the top with a well-constructed 107, displaying remarkable composure and stroke play. Latham anchored the innings brilliantly, remaining unbeaten on 118, ensuring his team reached a commanding total. However, the real acceleration came in the final phase, thanks to Phillips' explosive 61 off just 39 balls, which propelled New Zealand past the 300-run mark. The duo of Latham and Phillips added 113 runs in the last 10 overs, completely shifting the momentum in their favor.

New Zealand have put up an imposing total of 320/5 in their 50 overs after being asked to bat first by Pakistan. This is their second-highest total in Champions Trophy history, powered by sensational centuries from Will Young and Tom Latham and a blistering cameo from Glenn Phillips.

A triple to end the innings then! Haris Rauf bangs this one short and on leg, Tom Latham pulls it towards deep square leg. The fielder from deep mid-wicket tries to pick it up but lets it through. Commentary.Commentary: All in readiness now! Adding to the already electrifying atmosphere, an air show is underway, with jets soaring through the sky in formation, leaving behind trails in Pakistan’s national colors. The players are already out in the middle. Will Young and Devon Conway are the two openers of New Zealand. Shaheen Afridi has the new ball in hand and is raring to go. Let's play...

We are moments away from the start of the Champions Trophy 2025. However, before we get going, the players from both sides make their way out to the middle and line up for their respective national anthems. It will be New Zealand's first followed by the national anthem of Pakistan.

PITCH REPORT - Bazid Khan and Matthew Hayden is pitchside. They say that the pitch is dry but good for batting. Adds that you need to score 300 or more to defend. Mentions that there are some dry patches but also a bit of grass. Says that there is a nice breeze blowing and it is a good weather for the players. Ends by saying that the straight hit is 79m and the bowlers will need to protect the square boundaries.

New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner acknowledges the presence of dew, which could make batting easier later, but emphasizes the need for his team to bat well upfront. He highlights the valuable experience of playing with new faces in the squad and believes the team is well-prepared. Having faced their opponents frequently in both home and away conditions, Santner stresses the importance of assessing the conditions in Karachi and using them to their advantage.

Mohammad Rizwan, the skipper of Pakistan, says that they have seen in the last couple of matches that the dew comes later on so they want to utilize that. Adds that if they will think more of kinda playing with a tag of defending champions then it will put more pressure on them so they are just keeping it simple and aren’t thinking too much. Mentions that the Tri-series helped them prepare for this big tournament as they did everything there from bowling first to batting first. Further adds that he doesn’t want to repeat the mistakes of that final and informs that Haris Rauf is fully fit and he will replace Faheem Ashraf in the team.

New Zealand (Playing XI) - Devon Conway, Will Young, Kane Williamson, Daryl Mitchell, Tom Latham (WK), Glenn Phillips, Michael Bracewell, Mitchell Santner (C), Nathan Smith, Matt Henry, Will O’Rourke.
Pakistan (Playing XI) - Fakhar Zaman, Babar Azam, Saud Shakeel, Mohammad Rizwan (C/WK), Salman Agha, Tayyab Tahir, Khushdil Shah, Shaheen Afridi, Naseem Shah, Haris Rauf, Abrar Ahmed.

History favours New Zealand in the Champions Trophy, as they have won all three previous meetings against Pakistan in this tournament’s history. However, playing at home comes with both advantages and pressures for Pakistan, who will be desperate to reverse that record. The pitch is expected to be batting-friendly, but an early movement for pacers could make the first few overs tricky. With dew likely to play a role in the evening, chasing might be the preferred option for the team winning the toss. The weather forecast looks clear, setting the stage for an exciting tournament opener. Don’t go anywhere as the toss and playing XI aren’t far away!

New Zealand, on the other hand, look well-balanced and in solid form. Kane Williamson has been in exceptional touch, leading from the front in batting up-front with consistency in the Tri-series. Alongside him, the likes of Devon Conway and Daryl Mitchell add stability and experience to their batting unit. The Kiwis also have a promising young pacer in Will O’Rourke, whose express pace and extra bounce make him a serious threat, especially under Karachi’s lights. Bowling remains one of their strongest assets, with Mitchell Santner leading the spin attack, a department where he has been among the best in white-ball cricket. Rachin Ravindra’s inclusion remains uncertain after sustaining a forehead injury, but New Zealand have solid replacements ready if needed.

Pakistan's squad has firepower, but a few concerns linger. Fakhar Zaman is in sublime form, and the team will rely heavily on his aggressive stroke play at the top where he will want to replicate his performance as he did in the final of the Champions Trophy 2017. Babar Azam’s recent form has been patchy, but as a player known for delivering on the big stage, Pakistan will hope that he can find his rhythm in this crucial opener. With Saim Ayub ruled out due to injury, Babar and Fakhar will open the innings. Bowling remains Pakistan’s strong suit, but Haris Rauf’s availability is uncertain due to a side strain. If he doesn’t play, they might play out the same XI that played in the Tri-series final. The experience of Shaheen Afridi and Naseem Shah will be crucial in leading the pace attack, while lone premier spinner Abrar Ahmed will play a key role in the middle overs.

The National Stadium in Karachi is all set to host a high-voltage clash which is the first match of Champions Trophy 2025 between Pakistan and New Zealand. Hello and welcome all of you, as the crowd is filling up in more numbers to support the defending champions and co-hosts, Pakistan, who will be eager to kickstart their campaign on a winning note, but New Zealand will be brimming with confidence, having recently defeated them in the final of the Tri-series. With both teams placed in Group A, every match holds immense significance, as a single slip-up could make the road to the playoffs tougher and get out of the tournament. New Zealand have dominated Pakistan in recent encounters, winning three of their last five games, including both clashes earlier this month. Pakistan, however, will be looking to turn the tide, especially in home conditions.

A hush falls over the fans. For eight long years, the world has waited, and now, the moment is finally upon us. The ICC Champions Trophy is back! This year's tournament is more than just a contest, it's like a homecoming. It returns to Pakistan, the land of passionate fans and the proud home of the defending champions, marking a momentous occasion with them hosting an ICC tournament since 1996. But the story doesn't end there. Adding to the global excitement and some touch of geopolitics as well, the vibrant city of Dubai joins the party as co-host, ready to welcome some exciting matches, including those exclusively featuring the cricketing powerhouse, India. With the main World Cup still a couple of years away, this Champions Trophy serves as the perfect prelude, igniting the cricketing spirit and keeping the energy of the sport at a fever pitch. Across four iconic venues - Karachi, Rawalpindi, Lahore, and Dubai - eight elite teams will clash, across two groups of four teams each, with their eyes on the ultimate prize. However, the venue for the finale is yet to be decided. For the staters then, the National Stadium of Karachi is all in readiness to host the curtain raiser as hosts and the defending champions Pakistan take on the challenging New Zealand side. Both teams recently clashed in a Triangular Series that also included South Africa which was won by the Kiwis by defeating the hosts in the finale. Pakistan has done decently in the limited overs formats since a year or two, but at home. Babar Azam is expected to open with Fakhar Zaman, due to Saim Ayub’s injury. While Saud Shakeel and captain Mohammad Rizwan are expected to be the middle order maestros with Salman Agha providing that depth. Rizwan and Salman are probably Pakistan’s best middle order batters right now, further evidenced by their record-breaking partnership against South Africa which led them to the tri-series finale. Also, the biggest thing to watch out for is Babar Azam's form, as the right-handed batter has just two fifty-plus scores to show in the last ten innings. The bowling narrative tells a different tale. The once-feared pace arsenal of Shaheen-Rauf-Naseem seeks its lethal edge again, while a thin spin department rests heavily on Abrar Ahmed's shoulders as the only frontline turner. Yet Pakistan's recent ODI conquests across Australia, Zimbabwe, and South Africa signal their big-match temperament remains intact. New Zealand's cricket story blends proven pedigree with fresh firepower. The 2000 Champions Trophy winners arrive with Mitchell Santner at the helm, backed by unmatched recent experience in Pakistani conditions - 11 ODIs since 2019. While injury forces Ben Sears out, the pace department gains fresh energy through Jacob Duffy and Nathan Smith who join the established seamer, Matt Henry with Will O’Rourke as another highly touted pacer in the mix. Lockie Ferguson's injury came in as a huge blow for the Kiwis and now they have named Kyle Jamieson as the replacement. Their velocity and variety offer captain Mitchell Santner multiple weapons against the subcontinental batters. At the heart of their campaign stands Kane Williamson – the only player linking back to their 2013 and 2017 Champions Trophy campaigns.
